<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
One might try to prove the result first for generic coefficients and
then introduce relations. However, specialisation can introduce common factors
in the cancellation step of mutation and change the denominators of the
exchange Laurent polynomials. A proof for the generic case therefore does
not automatically give a proof for all linear seeds.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
Every linear LP algebra over a unique factorisation domain is of finite type.
More precisely, for a linear seed \eqref{eq:linear}, the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every cluster variable not associated over $A$ to an initial variable
divides a nonzero $Y_I$ in $\mathcal U$.
\item Let $Q$ denote the product of all nonzero principal minors of $M$, that is,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:QH}
 Q=\prod_{\substack{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq[n]\\Y_I\ne0}}Y_I.
\end{equation}
Set $H = (x_1\cdots x_n)Q$. Then $H/v\in\mathcal U$ for every cluster variable $v$.
\item If $s$ is the number of distinct irreducible factors of $Q$ in
$A[x_1^{\pm1},\ldots,x_n^{\pm1}]$, up to units of this Laurent ring, then
there are at most $n+s$ cluster-variable classes up to $A^\times$ and at most
$\binom{n+s}{n}$ seed-equivalence classes. These admit a finite normalisation.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
A \emph{seed} is a tuple $S=(\mathbf x,\mathbf f)$, where
$\mathbf x=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ is a set of algebraically independent
generators of $\mathcal F$ over $K$, and
$\mathbf f=\{f^1,\ldots,f^n\}\subset A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(LP\arabic*)]
\item Each $f^\ell$ is irreducible and is not divisible by a cluster variable.
\item The polynomial $f^\ell$ does not involve $x_\ell$.
\end{enumerate}
Here irreducible means nonzero, a nonunit, and not a product of two nonunits.
We call $\mathbf x$ the \emph{cluster}, its elements \emph{cluster variables},
and the $f^\ell$ \emph{exchange polynomials}. The rank of the seed is $n$.
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- defn-2: body_md -->
\label{def:hat}
The exchange Laurent polynomial associated to $f^\ell$ has the form
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hat}
 \widehat{f^{\ell}}=f^\ell\prod_{t\ne\ell}x_t^{-e_{\ell t}},
 \qquad e_{\ell t}\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}.
\end{equation}
The exponents are uniquely determined by requiring, for every $t\ne\ell$,
that
\[
 \widehat{f^{\ell}}\big|_{x_t\leftarrow f^t/\xi}
 \in A[x_1^{\pm1},\ldots,x_{t-1}^{\pm1},\xi^{\pm1},
             x_{t+1}^{\pm1},\ldots,x_n^{\pm1}]
\]
and that this element is not divisible by $f^t$ in that ring.
<!-- end defn-2 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:denominator}
If $e_{\ell t}>0$, then $f^t$ does not involve $x_\ell$.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Write $f^\ell=\sum_{r\geq0}b_rx_t^r$, with $b_r$ independent of $x_t$.
By (LP1), $b_0\ne0$. Divisibility of
$\sum_rb_r(f^t)^r\xi^{-r}$ by $f^t$ implies divisibility of its constant
coefficient $b_0$. This divisibility can be checked in the polynomial ring, since
localising at coordinate variables does not invert any factor of $f^t$.
But $b_0$ is independent of $x_\ell$ by (LP2). Additivity of polynomial
degree over a domain shows that its factor $f^t$ is also independent of
$x_\ell$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- defn-3: body_md -->
\label{def:mutation}
	Mutation at index $i$ replaces $S$ by $S_i=(\mathbf y_i,\mathbf f_i)$. The procedure operates as follows. The cluster is
\[
 \mathbf y_i=\{x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1},y_i,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_n\},
 \qquad x_iy_i=\widehat{f^{i}}.
\]
We refer to the variables $x_i$, $y_i$ as \emph{mutation partners}. We set $f_i^i=f^i$. For $\ell\ne i$, if $f^\ell$ is independent of $x_i$,
we take $f_i^\ell\sim_A f^\ell$. Otherwise, we perform the following three steps:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Substitution.} Put
\[
 Z=\widehat{f^{i}}\big|_{x_\ell\leftarrow0},\qquad
 G=f^\ell\big|_{x_i\leftarrow Z/y_i}.
\]
\item \emph{Cancellation.} In the Laurent ring in the new coordinates,
take $G$ and remove all occurrences of each prime factor of $Z$.
\item \emph{Normalisation.} Take the polynomial representative
\eqref{eq:pol} of the result. This gives $f_i^\ell$ up to a unit of $A$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defn-3 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:mutation}
Mutation produces a valid seed and is reversible with suitable choices of
units. Moreover, $f^\ell$ depends on $x_i$ if and only if $f_i^\ell$ depends
on $y_i$, and $\widehat{f_i^i}=\widehat{f^{i}}$.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
These are the mutation properties established in
\cite[Section~2.2, in particular Lemma~2.11 and
Propositions~2.15--2.16]{lam2012laurent}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- defn-4: body_md -->
Two seeds are \emph{equivalent} if, after appropriately matching cluster variables to exchange polynomials in each seed, corresponding variables and exchange polynomials are
associated over $A$ as elements of $\mathcal F$. We write $[S]$ for the equivalence
class of $S$.
<!-- end defn-4 -->
<!-- defn-5: body_md -->
A Laurent phenomenon algebra $\mathcal A=(\mathcal A,\mathbf S)$ consists of a connected
mutation pattern of seeds $\mathbf S$ in $\mathcal F$, closed under mutation with
specified unit choices, together with the $A$-subalgebra $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal F$
generated by its cluster variables. The notation $\mathcal A(S)$ indicates a chosen
initial seed $S$ in this pattern.
<!-- end defn-5 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:laurent}
For any seed $T$ of an LP algebra $\mathcal A$, every cluster variable is an element
of $\mathcal L(T)$. In particular, $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal L(T)$.
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
This is \cite[Theorem~5.1]{lam2012laurent}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- defn-6: body_md -->
\label{def:finite}
A pattern is \emph{normalised} if it contains exactly one representative of
each of its seed-equivalence classes. A \emph{normalisation} of a pattern is
a mutation-compatible choice of equivalent representative seeds. An LP
algebra is \emph{of finite type} if it admits a normalisation with finitely
many seeds.
<!-- end defn-6 -->
<!-- defn-7: body_md -->
The \emph{upper LP algebra} and the \emph{upper bound at a seed $T$} are
\[
 \mathcal U=\bigcap_{T'\in\mathbf S}\mathcal L(T'),\qquad
 \operatorname{UB}(T)=\mathcal L(T)\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^n\mathcal L(\mu_iT).
\]
All intersections take place in $\mathcal F$. The Laurent phenomenon gives
$\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal U\subseteq\operatorname{UB}(T)$.
<!-- end defn-7 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:intersection}
For the path \eqref{eq:caterpillar},
\[
 \mathcal L_1\cap\mathcal L_3\subseteq\mathcal L_0,
 \qquad \mathcal L_0\cap\mathcal L_2\subseteq\mathcal L_3.
\]
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
If $h\in\mathcal L_1\cap\mathcal L_3$, then, since $x,y$ and the suppressed coordinates
are units in $\mathcal L_0$, we may write
\[
 h=\frac{a}{z^r}=\frac{b}{u^sv^t},\qquad
 a,b\in\mathcal L_0,\quad r,s,t\geq0.
\]
The equality $au^sv^t=bz^r$, primality of $z$, and
\eqref{eq:caterpillar-input} imply $z^r\mid a$ in $\mathcal L_0$. Thus
$h\in\mathcal L_0$. Reversing the path proves the other inclusion.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:upper}
For every seed $T$, one has $\operatorname{UB}(T)=\mathcal U$.
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $T'=\mu_kT$. For $j\ne k$, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:intersection} to
\[
 \mu_jT\xrightarrow{j}T\xrightarrow{k}T'\xrightarrow{j}\mu_jT'.
\]
It gives
\[
 \mathcal L(\mu_jT)\cap\mathcal L(T')\subseteq\mathcal L(\mu_jT'),\qquad
 \mathcal L(T)\cap\mathcal L(\mu_jT')\subseteq\mathcal L(\mu_jT).
\]
Together with the two common rings $\mathcal L(T)$ and $\mathcal L(T')$, these inclusions
show that $\operatorname{UB}(T)=\operatorname{UB}(T')$. In rank one the equality is immediate from
involutivity. Connectedness now shows that this common upper bound lies in
every Laurent ring of the pattern, and hence in $\mathcal U$. The reverse inclusion
is part of the definition.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:prime}
Every cluster variable is prime in $\mathcal U$, and $\mathcal U^\times=A^\times$.
More precisely,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:prime-ideal}
 q_i\mathcal U=\mathcal U\cap g^i\mathcal L_i,
 \qquad \nu_i(h)>0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ h\in q_i\mathcal U
 \quad(0\ne h\in\mathcal U).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The coordinate $q_i$ is a unit in the Laurent ring of its seed and in every
first neighbouring ring except $\mathcal L_i$. In $\mathcal L_i$, it is a unit times $g^i$.
Consequently, if $h\in\mathcal U\cap g^i\mathcal L_i$, then $h/q_i$ belongs to every
Laurent ring defining the upper bound at this seed. By
Proposition~\ref{prop:upper}, $h/q_i\in\mathcal U$. The other containment in
\eqref{eq:prime-ideal} is immediate. The contracted ideal on the right is
proper and prime, so $q_i$ is a prime nonunit of $\mathcal U$. The valuation
criterion follows as well.

If $h\in\mathcal U^\times$, its expression as a unit of $\mathcal L(T)$ is
$h=\epsilon\prod_jq_j^{\beta_j}$, with $\epsilon\in A^\times$ and
$\beta_j\in\mathbb Z$. Both $h$ and $h^{-1}$ belong to $\mathcal L_i$. Equation
\eqref{eq:valuation-coordinates} gives $\beta_i\geq0$ and $-\beta_i\geq0$
for every $i$. Thus $h=\epsilon$. Conversely every coefficient unit is
plainly a unit of $\mathcal U$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:residues}
Reduction modulo $P$ in the neighbouring chart $B[(v')^{\pm1}]$ induces a
homomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rho}
 \rho:\mathcal U\longrightarrow (B/(P))[T],\qquad
 \ker\rho=v\mathcal U,\qquad \rho(v')=T,
\end{equation}
where $T$ is an indeterminate.
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
For $h\in\mathcal U$, write $h=\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}b_rv^r$ in $B[v^{\pm1}]$, with
only finitely many nonzero $b_r\in B$. In the neighbouring chart,
\[
 h=\sum_r b_rE^r(v')^{-r}.
\]
Since $h\in B[(v')^{\pm1}]$, uniqueness of Laurent coefficients implies
$b_rE^r\in B$ for every $r$. Reduce coefficients modulo $P$, and denote
the image of $v'$ by $T$. Each term $b_rE^r(v')^{-r}$ then maps to
$\overline{b_rE^r}T^{-r}$. For $r>0$, the coefficient is divisible by $P$
and hence vanishes, so only terms with $r\leq0$ survive. The image is
therefore polynomial, not merely Laurent, in $T$.

The kernel is $\mathcal U\cap PB[(v')^{\pm1}]=v\mathcal U$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:prime}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:residue}
In the rank-two seed over $\mathbb Z$ with exchange polynomials $1+x_2$ and $1+x_1$, set
$v=x_1$, $v'=(1+x_2)/x_1$, and $B=\mathbb Z[x_2^{\pm1}]$.
Reduction modulo $P=1+x_2$ gives
\[
 \rho(x_1)=0,\qquad \rho(x_2)=-1,\qquad \rho(v')=T.
\]
The cluster variable $(1+x_1+x_2)/(x_1x_2)=(1+v')/x_2$ has residue
$-(1+T)$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
This construction specialises to the determinants of Lam and
Pylyavskyy \cite[Section~4.2, Proposition~4.5]{lam2016linear}. In their graph
setting, $a_0^\ell=A_\ell$ are independent coefficient indeterminates and
$a_t^\ell$ is $1$ or $0$ according as $\ell\to t$ is an edge or not. Their
matrix has diagonal entries $(A_\ell+\sum_{\ell\to t}x_t)/x_\ell$ and
off-diagonal entries $-1$ on edges. Its principal minors are their
acyclic-function generating functions $Y_I$, with the same notation used
here. For strongly connected $I$, these are precisely the noninitial
cluster variables \cite[Theorem~1.1]{lam2016linear}. The graph-case $Y_I$
also occur in the cluster-monomial basis theorem of
Dantas e Moura, Telekicherla Kandalam, and Woodruff \cite{dantas2025}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:minors-upper}
Every $z_\ell$, and hence every $Y_I$, lies in $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal U$.
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
If $y_\ell$ is obtained by mutating $x_\ell$, then
\[
 z_\ell=\frac{f^\ell}{x_\ell}
 =y_\ell\prod_{t\ne\ell}x_t^{e_{\ell t}}\in\mathcal A.
\]
The determinant $Y_I$ is a polynomial over $A$ in the $z_\ell$, so it also
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Apply the Laurent phenomenon.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:ranktwo-minors}
For $f^1=1+x_2$ and $f^2=1+x_1$ over $\mathbb Z$,
\[
 M=\begin{pmatrix}(1+x_2)/x_1&-1\\-1&(1+x_1)/x_2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its three nonempty principal minors are
\[
 Y_{\{1\}}=\frac{1+x_2}{x_1},\qquad
 Y_{\{2\}}=\frac{1+x_1}{x_2},\qquad
 Y_{\{1,2\}}=\frac{1+x_1+x_2}{x_1x_2}.
\]
In this example the minors themselves are precisely the noninitial cluster
variables. In general it is their prime factors that matter.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:forests}
Put $N=M\operatorname{diag}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. Give $\ell\to t$ weight
$w_{\ell t}=a_t^\ell x_t$ for $t\ne0$, and $\ell\to0$ weight
$w_{\ell0}=a_0^\ell$. The augmented matrix
\[
 \widetilde N=
 \begin{pmatrix}N&-(a_0^\ell)_{\ell\in[n]}\\0&0\end{pmatrix}
\]
is the row Laplacian of this weighted graph. Applying the principal-minor
case of the all-minors matrix-tree theorem \cite{chaiken1982}, with the
transpose convention for a row Laplacian, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:forest-expansion}
 \left(\prod_{\ell\in I}x_\ell\right)Y_I
 =\det N_{I,I}
 =\sum_{F\in\mathcal T_I}\ \prod_{(\ell\to t)\in F}w_{\ell t}.
\end{equation}
Here $\mathcal T_I$ consists of spanning directed forests rooted at
$([n]\cup\{0\})\setminus I$.
Thus the determinantal
numerators are weighted rooted-forest polynomials. The identity holds over
$A$ by specialisation of the polynomial identity in formal edge weights.
The next proposition additionally rules out total cancellation when the
coefficients satisfy relations; we give a direct leading-term argument.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- defn-8: body_md -->
\label{def:closed}
A \emph{closed homogeneous component} is a nonempty strongly connected
subset $J\subseteq[n]$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:closed}
 a_0^\ell=0\quad(\ell\in J),\qquad
 a_t^\ell=0\quad(\ell\in J,\ t\notin J).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, it is a sink strongly connected component of $\Gamma$ other
than $\{0\}$.
<!-- end defn-8 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:nonzero}
For a nonempty $I\subseteq[n]$, the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $Y_I\ne0$ as a rational function in the initial coordinates;
\item every vertex of $I$ has a directed path to $([n]\cup\{0\})\setminus I$;
\item $I$ contains no closed homogeneous component.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
If a vertex cannot reach the complement of $I$, all vertices reachable from
it lie in $I$. A sink strongly connected component of this reachable
subgraph has no outgoing edge in the full graph and is a closed homogeneous
component. Conversely, a vertex of a closed component cannot leave it.
This proves the equivalence of (2) and (3).

Suppose $J\subseteq I$ is a closed homogeneous component. Order the vertices
of $J$ before those of $I\setminus J$. The block in the rows of $J$ and
columns of $I\setminus J$ is zero, so $M_{I,I}$ is block triangular.
Furthermore, \eqref{eq:linear-system} gives
\[
 M_{J,J}(x_\ell)_{\ell\in J}=0.
\]
This is a nonzero kernel vector over $\mathcal F$. Thus $Y_J=0$ and $Y_I=0$.

It remains to show that (2) implies (1), including when the coefficients
have signs or satisfy relations. Consider the polynomial matrix
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Nmatrix}
 N_I=M_{I,I}\operatorname{diag}(x_t:t\in I),\qquad
 (N_I)_{\ell\ell}=f^\ell,\quad
 (N_I)_{\ell t}=-a_t^\ell x_t\ (\ell\ne t).
\end{equation}
For $\ell\in I$, let $d_\ell$ be the shortest directed distance to the
complement of $I$, and put $d_t=0$ outside $I$, including at $0$.
Choose pairwise distinct real numbers $\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_n$ in
$(0,1/3)$ and assign weights
\[
 \omega_t=-d_t+\epsilon_t\quad(t\ne0),\qquad \omega_0=0
\]
to $x_t$. These are auxiliary weights on formal monomials, not values of
the coefficients. Every neighbour of $\ell$ has distance at least
$d_\ell-1$, and one has distance exactly $d_\ell-1$. Hence there is a unique
neighbour $t(\ell)$ of greatest weight and its distance is $d_\ell-1$.

Let $e_\ell$ denote the standard row vectors with positions indexed by $I$.
Row $\ell$ of $N_I$ is the sum, over its outgoing edges, of
\[
 a_t^\ell x_t(e_\ell-e_t)\quad(t\in I),\qquad
 a_t^\ell x_te_\ell\quad(t\notin I).
\]
The same formula includes the edge to $0$ since $x_0=1$.
Choose in each row the summand indexed by $t(\ell)$. Its edge strictly
decreases distance. In an ordering by distance, the matrix of the selected
row vectors is triangular with diagonal entries one. Thus its determinant
is one. By multilinearity in the rows, the unique choice of largest total
weight contributes
\begin{equation}\label{eq:leading-tree}
 \prod_{\ell\in I}a_{t(\ell)}^\ell x_{t(\ell)}
\end{equation}
to $\det N_I$. Every other choice has smaller total weight. The coefficient
in \eqref{eq:leading-tree} is nonzero because $A$ is an integral domain. This term
cannot cancel, so $\det N_I\ne0$ and $Y_I\ne0$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:cofactor}
Let $J$ be a closed homogeneous component and let $i\in J$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cofactor}
 Y_{J\setminus\{i\}}\ne0,\qquad
 Z_{J,i}:=\frac{Y_{J\setminus\{i\}}}{x_i}\in\mathcal U.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
A singleton closed component would have $f^i=0$, contrary to (LP1). Hence
$|J|\geq2$, and $I=J\setminus\{i\}$ is nonempty. Every vertex of $I$ can
reach $i$ inside $J$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:nonzero} gives $Y_I\ne0$.
Since the exchanges in the rows of $J$ involve only coordinates in $J$,
\[
 D_I:=\Bigl(\prod_{t\in I}x_t\Bigr)Y_I
       =\det N_I\in A[x_t:t\in J].
\]
The sum of row $\ell\in I$ of $N_I$ is $a_i^\ell x_i$.
After setting $x_i=0$, every row sum is zero. The nonempty matrix then has
the all-ones vector in its kernel, so its determinant is zero.
It follows that $x_i\mid D_I$ in the polynomial ring. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cofactor-laurent}
 Z_{J,i}=\frac{D_I/x_i}{\prod_{t\in I}x_t}
\end{equation}
is polynomial in $x_i$ and Laurent in the other initial coordinates.

In the first neighbouring chart at $i$, substitute $x_i=\widehat{f^{i}}/y_i$ into
\eqref{eq:cofactor-laurent}. Since there is no negative power of $x_i$,
the result is Laurent. In every other first neighbouring chart, $Y_I$ is
Laurent by Lemma~\ref{lem:minors-upper} and $x_i$ is an unchanged unit.
Hence $Z_{J,i}\in\operatorname{UB}(S)=\mathcal U$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:upper}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:minor-divisibility}
Let $S$ be the linear seed \eqref{eq:linear}. If a cluster variable $v$ is
not associated over $A$ to any initial coordinate, then
\[
 Y_I\ne0,\qquad \frac{Y_I}{v}\in\mathcal U
\]
for some nonempty $I\subseteq[n]$.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Suppose, for a contradiction, that $v$ divides no nonzero principal minor
in $\mathcal U$. Choose a seed containing $v$, let $v'$ be its mutation partner,
and use the notation $B,P$ of \eqref{eq:residue-chart}. Compose the map of
Lemma~\ref{lem:residues} with the inclusion into $k[T]$, where
$k=\operatorname{Frac}(B/(P))$. Denote the composite again by $\rho$, so that
\[
 \rho:\mathcal U\longrightarrow k[T],\qquad \ker\rho=v\mathcal U,
 \qquad \rho(v')=T.
\]
Write
\[
 X_\ell=\rho(x_\ell),\qquad W_\ell=\rho(z_\ell).
\]
All these polynomials are nonzero. Indeed, $X_\ell=0$ would imply
$v\mid x_\ell$ in $\mathcal U$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:prime}, both are prime, so they
would be associated by a unit of $\mathcal U$, hence by a unit of $A$, contrary to
the choice of $v$. Also $z_\ell=Y_{\{\ell\}}\ne0$, so $W_\ell=0$ would
contradict the assumption that $v$ divides no nonzero minor.

At least one $X_\ell$ has positive degree in $T$. To see this, observe that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:localise}
 \mathcal U[x_1^{-1},\ldots,x_n^{-1}]
 =A[x_1^{\pm1},\ldots,x_n^{\pm1}]=\mathcal L(S).
\end{equation}
The two inclusions follow from $A[\mathbf x]\subseteq\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal L(S)$.
Since every $X_\ell\ne0$, $\rho$ extends to this localisation with values
in $k(T)$. If all the $X_\ell$ were constant, the image of $\mathcal L(S)$ would
lie in $k$. But the Laurent phenomenon puts $v'$ in $\mathcal L(S)$, whereas
$\rho(v')=T\notin k$. This is impossible.

Set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:maximum-degree}
 d=\max_\ell\deg_T X_\ell>0,\qquad
 I=\{\ell:\deg_T X_\ell=d\}.
\end{equation}
Let bars denote the images of coefficients in $k$. Applying $\rho$ to
\eqref{eq:linear-system} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:residue-linear-system}
 X_\ell W_\ell=\overline{a_0^\ell}
       +\sum_{t\ne\ell}\overline{a_t^\ell}X_t.
\end{equation}
For $\ell\in I$, the right side has degree at most $d$. The left side is
a nonzero product, and $\deg_T X_\ell=d$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:constant-W}
 W_\ell\in k^\times\qquad(\ell\in I).
\end{equation}
If $b_\ell\in k^\times$ is the leading coefficient of $X_\ell$ for
$\ell\in I$, comparing coefficients of $T^d$ in
\eqref{eq:residue-linear-system} yields
\[
 W_\ell b_\ell=
 \sum_{t\in I\setminus\{\ell\}}\overline{a_t^\ell}b_t.
\]
Therefore $\rho(M_{I,I})(b_\ell)_{\ell\in I}=0$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:singular-residue}
 \rho(Y_I)=0.
\end{equation}
If $Y_I\ne0$ in the original ambient field, then
\eqref{eq:singular-residue} says $v\mid Y_I$ in $\mathcal U$, the desired
contradiction.

It remains to deal with $Y_I=0$ identically. This is different from merely
having zero residue. By Proposition~\ref{prop:nonzero}, there is a closed
homogeneous component $J\subseteq I$. For any $i\in J$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:cofactor} supplies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cofactor-identity}
 x_iZ_{J,i}=Y_{J\setminus\{i\}},\qquad
 Z_{J,i}\in\mathcal U,\qquad Y_{J\setminus\{i\}}\ne0.
\end{equation}
By our assumption, the right side has nonzero residue. Its residue is also
constant: its diagonal entries are among $W_\ell$ for $\ell\in I$, and
\eqref{eq:constant-W} applies. Reducing \eqref{eq:cofactor-identity} gives
\[
 X_i\rho(Z_{J,i})\in k^\times.
\]
But $\deg_T X_i=d>0$ and $\rho(Z_{J,i})\in k[T]$. A polynomial of positive
degree cannot multiply another polynomial to give a nonzero constant.
This final contradiction proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:common-multiple}
The element $H$ in \eqref{eq:QH} is nonzero and belongs to $\mathcal A$.
For every cluster variable $v$, $H/v\in\mathcal U$.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
All retained factors belong to $\mathcal A$ and are nonzero. If $v\sim_A x_i$, use
the factor $x_i$ of $H$. Otherwise Theorem~\ref{thm:minor-divisibility}
supplies a factor $Y_I$ of $Q$ with $Y_I/v\in\mathcal U$ and we multiply by the remaining
factors of $H$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:localised-primes}
A noninitial cluster variable $v$ is a prime nonunit in $\mathcal L_0$ and satisfies
$\nu_i(v)=0$ for every $i$. If two noninitial cluster variables are associated
in $\mathcal L_0$, then they are associated over $A$.
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:prime}, $v$ and the $x_i$ are prime in $\mathcal U$, and $v$ is
not associated to any $x_i$. Hence $v$ divides no product of initial
coordinates. The prime ideal $v\mathcal U$ survives the localisation
\eqref{eq:localise}, so $v$ remains a prime nonunit in $\mathcal L_0$.

Likewise $x_i$ does not divide $v$ in $\mathcal U$. Since $v\in\mathcal U$, its valuation
$\nu_i(v)$ is nonnegative, and \eqref{eq:prime-ideal} shows that it is zero.
If $v=\epsilon x_1^{\beta_1}\cdots x_n^{\beta_n}w$ for another noninitial
variable $w$, with $\epsilon\in A^\times$, applying $\nu_i$ gives
$0=\beta_i$. Thus $v=\epsilon w$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:variable-count}
If $Q$ has $s$ distinct irreducible factors up to Laurent units, there are
at most $n+s$ cluster-variable classes up to $A^\times$.
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Every noninitial cluster variable divides $Q$ in $\mathcal U$, and hence in
$\mathcal L_0$, by Theorem~\ref{thm:minor-divisibility}. It is prime there by
Lemma~\ref{lem:localised-primes}, so it is associated to one of the $s$
irreducible factors of $Q$. The last assertion of the lemma says that two
different coefficient-unit classes cannot correspond to the same Laurent
prime. The initial variables contribute the remaining $n$ classes.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:rigidity}
Two seeds in one LP algebra whose clusters agree up to coefficient units
are equivalent.
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
First suppose the clusters agree exactly, with coordinates
$\mathbf q=\{q_1,\ldots,q_n\}$. Write the exchanges of the two seeds as
$g^i,h^i$, and their mutation partners at $i$ as
\[
 u=\frac{\widehat{g^i}}{q_i},\qquad
 w=\frac{\widehat{h^i}}{q_i}.
\]
Set $B_i=A[q_j^{\pm1}:j\ne i]$. Laurentness of $u$ in the neighbouring
chart $B_i[w^{\pm1}]$ and the equality
\[
 u=w\,\frac{\widehat{g^i}}{\widehat{h^i}}
\]
show that $\widehat{g^i}/\widehat{h^i}\in B_i$: this is the single
coefficient of $w$ in the Laurent expansion. Interchanging the two seeds
shows that the reciprocal is also in $B_i$. The ratio is therefore a unit
of $B_i$, namely a coefficient unit times a Laurent monomial in the $q_j$.
Taking polynomial representatives gives $g^i\sim_A h^i$ for every $i$.

If the clusters agree only up to coefficient units, express both sets of
exchange polynomials in the same rescaled coordinates. The Laurent rings
are unchanged, and the two displayed exchange relations acquire only
coefficient-unit factors. The same argument applies and gives equivalence
in the common ambient field.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:normalisation}
If an LP algebra of rank $n$ has $N<\infty$ cluster-variable classes, then it admits a normalisation with at most $\binom{N}{n}$ seeds.
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Choose one representative of each variable class. Every genuine cluster
determines a set $\mathcal C$ of $n$ chosen representatives. Coordinates
in one cluster cannot be associated, by algebraic independence.
Lemma~\ref{lem:rigidity} says that $\mathcal C$ determines a single
seed-equivalence class. Mutation compatibility therefore determines, for
each $u\in\mathcal C$, the class of its mutation partner. Let $v$ be the
chosen representative of that class.

The product $uv$ is a coefficient-unit multiple of the exchange Laurent
polynomial in that direction, expressed in the coordinates
$\mathcal C\setminus\{u\}$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:chosen-exchange}
 g_{\mathcal C,u}=\operatorname{pol}_{\mathcal C}(uv).
\end{equation}
These exchanges give a valid seed $S_{\mathcal C}$ equivalent to the
original class. Indeed, in each direction we have just rescaled coordinates and
multiplied an ordinary exchange polynomial by a coefficient unit.
The normalisation exponents are unaffected by these unit changes.
Consequently, the exchange Laurent polynomial of
$g_{\mathcal C,u}$ is exactly $uv$, and mutating $u$ inserts exactly $v$.

Put $\mathcal C'=(\mathcal C\setminus\{u\})\cup\{v\}$. By mutation
compatibility, a mutation of $S_{\mathcal C}$ at $u$ is equivalent to
$S_{\mathcal C'}$. In all other directions the unit choices in mutation
allow us to select precisely the exchanges of $S_{\mathcal C'}$.
At the replaced coordinate the polynomial is required to remain unchanged.
This too holds exactly, since $uv$ is independent of both $u$ and $v$, and the
other coordinates are unchanged. Hence
\[
 g_{\mathcal C,u}=\operatorname{pol}_{\mathcal C}(uv)
 =\operatorname{pol}_{\mathcal C'}(vu)=g_{\mathcal C',v}.
\]
Thus these representative seeds form a mutation-closed pattern. It is
connected as the image of the original pattern and has at most
$\binom{N}{n}$ seeds.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:minor-divisibility} proves (1), and
Corollary~\ref{cor:common-multiple} proves (2).
Proposition~\ref{prop:variable-count} gives at most $n+s$ variable classes.
Proposition~\ref{prop:normalisation} supplies a finite normalisation and
the seed bound in (3). This proves finite type.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
